'''''Dryopteris aemula''''', the '''hay-scented buckler-fern'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2014-10-17 }}</ref> or '''hay-scented fern''', is a species of perennial [[Leptosporangiate fern|leptosporangiate]] [[fern]].

==Description==
{{One source|date=June 2026}}
''Dryopteris aemula'' grows as a crown of [[fronds]] arising from a short ascending [[rhizome]].

The [[rachis]] is dark purple-brown with red-brown lanceolate scales. Leaves are [[Pinnation|tri-pinnate]], triangular-[[Ovate (botany)|ovate]] or triangular-[[lanceolate]], {{convert|15–60|cm|in|abbr=on}} long, often arching, semi-evergreen and pale yellow-green. Scattered small sessile glands grow on the underside or both surfaces of the fronds. [[Pinnation|Pinnae]] are slightly concave giving the frond a characteristic crisped appearance. The plant is hay-scented.

[[Sorus|Sori]] or spore-producing organs occur in a row down each side of the [[midrib]]. The indusium of the [[sorus]] is irregularly toothed and edged with sessile glands.

The plant does not reproduce vegetatively and relies upon [[spores]] to generate new individuals.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Quintanilla |first=Luis G. |last2=Escudero |first2=AdriáN |date=2006-09-01 |title=Spore Fitness Components Do Not Differ Between Diploid and Allotetraploid Species of Dryopteris (Dryopteridaceae) |url=http://academic.oup.com/aob/article/98/3/609/251661/Spore-Fitness-Components-Do-Not-Differ-Between |journal=Annals of Botany |language=en |volume=98 |issue=3 |pages=609–618 |doi=10.1093/aob/mcl137 |issn=1095-8290 |pmc=2803563 |pmid=16845140}}</ref>

==Distribution==
''Dryopteris aemula'' is confined to the atlantic coastal areas of western Europe and [[Macaronesia]]. ''D. aemula'' is highly oceanic in its distribution occurring mostly in the Köppen climate type [[Oceanic climate|Cfb]] (oceanic climates). Even within Great Britain, it is restricted to western districts and has just a few outlying eastern localities such as [[The Weald]].

''D. aemula'' reaches the northern limit of its distribution in Britain.

20% of the world population of ''D. aemula'' is in the United Kingdom.<ref>{{cite web |author1=Kent Biodiversity Action Plan Steering Group |title=Kent Biodiversity Action Plan |url=https://www.medway.gov.uk/download/downloads/id/279/kent_biodiversity_action_plan.pdf |website=[[Medway Council]] |access-date=21 November 2022 |date=1997}}</ref>
